source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds
finding: Speed bugs do not add to pilot memory. They let the cockpit system remember speeds by turning recall and scale reading into a judgement of spatial adjacency.
numbers: Ethnographic case study of MD-80 approach. Bugs set at 227 knots and up; PNF calls out when speed varies more than 5 knots from approach speed. No statistics.
quote: Speed bugs do not help pilots remember speeds; rather, they are part of the process by which the cockpit system remembers speeds.
limits: Qualitative, one aircraft type. Not an experiment.
agent_relevance: An agent's checks are not memory aids for the model. They reshape the task so the checker does a cheaper judgement (compare to a marker) instead of recall.

source: Hutchins (1995) cross-check procedure
finding: The crew cross-checks bug settings aloud with challenge/response ('Set on the left and cross-checked' / 'Set on the right and cross-checked'), against the speed card and each other's instrument.
numbers: Callout at 500 ft AFL: 'Five hundred feet, plus four, seven down' (4 knots fast, 700 ft/min). Cross-check repeated at slat extension, before-landing checklist, final approach.
limits: Redundancy is procedural; no error rates measured.
agent_relevance: Pattern for guardrails: an independent second party confirms a written setting, with a fixed phrase and a value, not a vague 'ok'.

source: Hutchins (1995) transposition errors and tool transformations
finding: Setting bugs needs reading a table, computing and moving a marker. Transposition errors are said to be the most frequent error in this step, so the system adds redundant checks there.
numbers: Text cites Norman 1991 and Wickens & Flach 1988 for transposition being the most frequent error type. No rate given in this paper.
limits: Claim is cited, not measured here.
agent_relevance: Put checks where the error-prone transform happens (copying a value), not only at the end.

source: Norman (1993) Things That Make Us Smart / Norman (1991) Cognitive artifacts
finding: Norman holds that artifacts change the task, not the person. Hutchins cites Norman 1993 for artifacts that give more than external memory. Seen only as citations in Hutchins; book not opened.
numbers: None seen.
limits: Secondary: seen only through Hutchins' reference list.
agent_relevance: Judge a scaffold by how it changes the task, not by whether it helps the model remember.

source: Haynes et al. (2009) WHO Surgical Safety Checklist, NEJM
finding: A 19-item checklist in 8 hospitals cut complications and deaths in a before/after design.
numbers: 3,733 patients before, 3,955 after. Deaths 1.5% to 0.8% (P=0.003). Inpatient complications within 30 days 11.0% to 7.0% (P<0.001).
limits: Before/after, no control group, no randomisation; Hawthorne effect possible; hospitals chosen for willingness.
agent_relevance: Human evidence that a short forced checklist cuts errors. Treat as an upper bound; effect depends on use.

source: Pronovost et al. (2006) Keystone ICU catheter infection checklist, NEJM
finding: A checklist for central line insertion cut bloodstream infections, sustained over 18 months.
numbers: 103 ICUs, 375,757 catheter-days. Median rate per 1,000 catheter-days 2.7 to 0 by 3 months. Incidence-rate ratio 0.62 (0.47-0.81) at 0-3 months, 0.34 (0.23-0.50) at 16-18 months.
limits: Mostly Michigan ICUs; no control arm; bundled with culture change and authority to stop.
agent_relevance: A checklist works with authority to stop. In an agent the program, not the model, must be able to block.

source: Urbach et al. (2014) Ontario surgical checklists, NEJM (via news summaries)
finding: A mandated checklist in Ontario found no significant fall in mortality or complications.
numbers: 101 hospitals; 109,341 procedures before vs 106,370 after. Mortality 0.71% to 0.65% (ns). Complications 3.86% to 3.82%.
limits: Seen through secondary reports only. 3-month follow-up, weak implementation; editorial says checklist likely not really used.
agent_relevance: A checklist that exists but is not enforced does nothing. Count checks by code, not by the model saying it did them.

source: Degani & Wiener (1993) Cockpit checklists: concepts, design, and use
finding: Field study of flight-deck checklists: format, length, use, human limits (skipped items pass unnoticed, production pressure, CRM).
numbers: 42 crews, 72 flights, about 140 flight hours (per a search summary). Two use modes: read-do, and do-from-memory then confirm.
limits: Seen only through search summary.
agent_relevance: Do-then-confirm suits an agent: act first, then a separate check, which keeps the check independent.

source: Huang et al. (2023) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without an external signal, asking the model to check its own answer does not help and can hurt. With oracle labels it helps a lot.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 standard, 75.1 round 2, 74.7 round 3; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5; CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 79.5. Oracle labels: GPT-3.5 HotpotQA 29.0 to 49.0 for the GPT-4 row as read. GPT-3.5 keeps its GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
limits: Intrinsic self-correction with generic prompts; some earlier gains came from oracle labels or weak first prompts.
agent_relevance: A model cross-checking its own text is not a second pilot. The check needs an outside signal (tool, test, other source).

source: Dhuliawala et al. (2023) Chain-of-Verification Reduces Hallucination
finding: Plan verification questions, answer them in a separate context (factored), then revise. Cuts hallucination.
numbers: Wikidata list precision 0.17 to 0.36 (Llama 65B); hallucinated answers 2.95 to 0.68. MultiSpanQA F1 0.39 to 0.48 (+23%). Longform FACTSCORE 55.9 to 71.4 (+28%); factored 63.7, factor+revise 71.4.
limits: Llama 65B; independence from the draft is what matters; does not fix reasoning errors.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM version of the cross-check: the second party answers without seeing the first party's text.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)
finding: Task verification failures are a main failure class in multi-agent systems; verifiers are often superficial.
numbers: 1,600+ annotated traces; 7 MAS frameworks, failure rate 41% to 86.7%. Verification failures: premature termination 6.20%, no/incomplete verification 8.20%, incorrect verification 9.10%. Annotator kappa 0.88; LLM annotator kappa 0.77.
quote: the presence of a verifier is not a silver bullet
limits: Open-source MAS; taxonomy is descriptive, not causal.
agent_relevance: A verifier that only checks that code compiles is a checklist item ticked without the check. Verify against the real rules.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces
finding: A custom tool interface (ACI) changes what the same model can do. Norman's thesis (tools reshape the task) tested directly on LLMs.
numbers: GPT-4 Turbo solves 12.47% of 2,294 SWE-bench tasks vs previous best 3.8%. Ablation on 300 Lite tasks: ACI beats shell-only by 10.7 points. Editor: linting 18.0 vs no lint 15.0 vs no edit tool 10.3. Search: summarized 18.0, none 15.7, iterative 12.0. Viewer 100 lines 18.0 vs full file 12.7.
limits: Tuned on GPT-4 Turbo; portable to Claude 3 Opus at 10.5%. Iterative search was worse than none.
agent_relevance: Design the tools and their feedback format. A linter guard on edits is a checklist inside the tool, worth +3 points.

source: Yao et al. (2023) ReAct
finding: Interleaving reasoning with actions that touch the world reduces hallucination and error propagation.
numbers: ALFWorld best ReAct trial 71% success; ReAct beats the internal-monologue variant 71 vs 53. ReAct plus CoT-SC combinations best on HotpotQA/FEVER.
limits: Few-shot prompting; ReAct alone was prone to repeated actions.
agent_relevance: The environment as external memory and check: the cockpit idea of reading state from the world.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: Verbal reflections stored in an episodic buffer after external feedback raise success.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 91% vs GPT-4 80%; AlfWorld +22% absolute over baseline in 12 iterations; HotPotQA +20%.
limits: Gains depend on an external signal (tests, environment reward), the same limit Huang names.
agent_relevance: Memory held outside the model in a notes buffer, like the speed card, with an outside check.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine
finding: Generate, give feedback, refine with the same model. Gains on many tasks.
numbers: About 20% absolute average improvement; 5-40% across tasks; up to 13% on code (abstract and intro).
limits: Contradicted on reasoning by Huang et al. when no external signal; TICK shows vanilla Self-Refine can degrade LiveBench.
agent_relevance: Self-feedback needs structure: see checklist feedback (TICK).

source: Cook et al. (2024) TICK: Generated checklists improve LLM evaluation and generation
finding: Instruction-specific YES/NO checklists, written by the model, make judging and refining more reliable.
numbers: Judge-human exact agreement 46.4% to 52.2%. STICK self-refinement on LiveBench reasoning +7.8% absolute; Best-of-N on WildBench +6.3%; Command-R+ InFoBench +6.5%, WildBench +7.1%. Vanilla Self-Refine degraded LiveBench.
limits: Checklist is generated by the same model; gains smaller on GPT-4o (+0.8% LiveBench).
agent_relevance: Strongest LLM evidence for checklists: decomposed binary items beat a holistic score.

source: Viswanathan et al. (2025) Checklists Are Better Than Reward Models (RLCF)
finding: Training with checklist-derived rewards beats reward models on instruction following.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: FollowBench hard satisfaction +5.4% relative, InFoBench +6.9% relative, Arena-Hard +6.4% relative; other gains 2.8%-8.4%.
limits: Trains weights, so not a scaffold; instruction-following tasks, 7B model.
agent_relevance: Checklist items give a measurable signal; our program can compute pass/fail per item.

source: Nye et al. (2021) Show Your Work: Scratchpads for Intermediate Computation
finding: Letting a model write intermediate steps into a scratchpad greatly improves multi-step computation, like a pilot writing numbers down.
numbers: Direct prediction 8.8% / 31.8% vs scratchpad 20.1% / 50.7% on one task (two columns as read); 11% / 20% vs 26.5% / 41.5% on another.
limits: Column meaning not fully checked; few-shot or fine-tuned models; errors still compound.
agent_relevance: Scratchpad is an external representation: the model reads its written state rather than recalling it.

source: Figueiredo (2025) Cognitive scaffolding for LLM instruction
finding: Removing symbolic structure or a short-term memory schema in a tutoring LLM degrades reasoning behaviours (search summary).
numbers: Five system variants, expert rubric; no numbers read.
limits: Synthetic users and LLM judges; not opened.
agent_relevance: Ablation form to copy: remove each scaffold part and measure.

source: Cognitive Workspace (2025) Active memory management for LLMs
finding: Applies extended-mind and Hutchins' distributed cognition to LLM memory; reports reuse of working-memory items vs RAG.
numbers: 58.6% average memory reuse (54-60% by task) vs 0% for traditional RAG; 17-18% net efficiency gain.
limits: Author-reported on own tasks, only abstract and intro skimmed; verify before citing.
agent_relevance: Explicit externalised working memory beat re-retrieval in their setup; unverified.

source: VeriLA (2025) verification framework for LLM agent failures
finding: Per-agent expectations plus a verifier trained on human gold standards flag faulty steps for human review.
numbers: Abstract gives no numbers; says the case study is interpretable and efficient.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Per-step human-designed criteria resemble role-specific checklist items.

source: AdaptiveCoPilot (2025) neuroadaptive LLM cockpit guidance
finding: An LLM adapts checklist training cues to measured pilot workload in a VR cockpit.
numbers: Formative study N=3 expert pilots; evaluation N=8 licensed pilots vs baseline and random feedback; more optimal workload states, shorter completion time.
limits: Tiny sample, VR training task; no effect size seen.
agent_relevance: LLM as part of the cockpit system, not a replacement for the checklist.

source: LeRAAT and Virtual Co-Pilot pilot-assistant LLMs (search summary)
finding: LLM cockpit assistants reported for procedure retrieval and situational analysis.
numbers: Virtual Co-Pilot: 90.5% situational analysis, 86.5% procedure retrieval (search summary).
limits: Not opened; self-reported.
agent_relevance: Retrieving the procedure from a card, not recall, matches the speed card design.

source: Auto-Eval Judge and Never Stop Thinking checklist evals (search summary)
finding: Per-item checklists with evidence checks are used to judge agent completion.
numbers: Two verifiers from different model families agreed on 87.9% of item judgements (summary only).
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Use verifiers from a different family to reduce correlated error.

source: Hollan, Hutchins & Kirsh (2000) Distributed cognition: toward a new foundation for HCI
finding: Extends the cockpit analysis to a general framework; not opened.
numbers: None read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Background only; no numbers claimed.

source: Synthesis: checklists work only when run, and models cannot self-grade
finding: Urbach (no effect when not enforced), Haynes and Pronovost (large effects when enforced) and Huang (self-check fails without outside signal) together say: enforce checks in code and use outside information.
numbers: Haynes 11.0% to 7.0% complications; Urbach 3.86% to 3.82%; Huang CSQA 75.8 to 38.1.
limits: Cross-domain synthesis; no direct LLM test.
agent_relevance: Supports guardrails run by the program with independent evidence.
